To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

metal-ligand distances can be well predicted from the Cambridge Structural Data Base, and metal-ligand coordination numbers can be predicted from idealized geometries, but that metal-ligands angles cannot.

the geometry of metal-lagand interactions in proteins determined at high resolution is consistent with that found in small-molecule complexes in the CSD, and that, with minor modifications, this information can be used as a target for validation of metal geometry or for restraints on geometry in refinement of structures determined at poorer resolution.
metal-ligand geometries in metalloprotein crystal structures can be validated or refined by reference to a small set of restraints derived from the Cambridge Structural Data Base (CSD).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a database of small-molecule structures and with the use of this database to provide information for validation or refinement of macromolecular crystal structures.
the use of information from the CSD in protein structure determination.
the geometry of metal-lion interactions in proteins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the metal-ligand geometry of proteins can be predicted with some confidence from the CSD.

metal coordination geometry in metalloproteins is well defined and that the CSD is a valuable guide in the interpretation of the geometry in structures determined at low resolution or in refinement of structures determined at higher resolution.
the geometry of metal coordination in proteins is well defined, but that there is a need for more high-resolution structures to provide reliable information about angles at the metal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metal-donor distances are reasonably well predicted from the CDS for ligands which mimic amino-acid side-chain groups in proteins, but that angles at the metal require more caution.
for metalloprotein structures determined to high resolution, geometry is well predicted from the C.S.D. for ligands which mimic amino-acid side-chain groups in proteins.

the metal-donor bond lengths and coordination numbers found in metalloproteins are in good agreement with the CSD data and that the CSD provides useful restraints for refinement of structures determined at poorer resolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Cambridge Structural Database is a valuable resource for the analysis and interpretation of protein structures.
the geometry of metal-lion interactions in proteins is not as flexible as has been assumed, and that it can be described in terms of the geometry of analogous small-molecule interactions.
the CSD can be used as a guide for validation and/or refinement of structures determined at lower resolution.
